meta.note: Every quantity is a number with a unit, a year and a source_id. Rank is derived at runtime, never stored.

materials.name: Silicon

annualProduction.note: silicon materials: ferrosilicon plus silicon metal

discovered.era: Isolated by Berzelius

facts.text: Semiconductor-grade silicon is refined to 99.9999999% purity, nine nines, among the purest bulk materials ever made.
Second only to oxygen in the crust, and the two are usually found bonded to each other as silica.
Oxygen and silicon alone are three-quarters of the crust by weight. The ground is mostly rusted glass.

pros: Can be made purer than almost anything else
Its electrical behaviour can be tuned atom by atom

materials.name: Aluminium

anthropogenicStock.note: in-use stock, part of the 39 Gt metals category

annualProduction.note: primary smelter production

discovered.era: Ørsted; commercially viable after Hall–Héroult, 1886

facts.text: Recycling aluminium takes about 5% of the energy needed to smelt it from ore, and the metal loses nothing in the process.
Before electrolysis made it cheap, aluminium outpriced gold; Napoleon III reserved aluminium cutlery for his most honoured guests.

pros: Light but still strong
Never really corrodes
Recycling it costs a twentieth of the energy
cons: Smelting it from ore is hugely power hungry
Weaker than steel for the same thickness

annualProduction.note: blast-furnace pig iron, the feedstock for most steel

discovered.era: Iron Age; meteoric iron worked far earlier

facts.text: Iron is the most abundant element in the Earth as a whole, most of it sank into the core while the planet was still molten.
Every iron atom heavier than nickel in your blood was forged in a dying star; the crust merely inherited it.

discovered.era: Isolated by Humphry Davy

facts.text: Magnesium is the lightest structural metal in common use, about two-thirds the density of aluminium.
Seawater holds roughly 1.3 kg of magnesium per tonne, which is where a good share of production comes from.

materials.name: Titanium

annualProduction.note: titanium sponge metal; titanium mineral concentrates run ~9 Mt/yr

discovered.era: Identified by Gregor; pure metal isolated 1910

facts.text: Titanium is the ninth most abundant element in the crust, yet it stayed a laboratory curiosity for a century because separating it from oxygen is brutally hard.
The SR-71 Blackbird was 85% titanium, and much of the ore was bought through intermediaries from the Soviet Union.

pros: Strongest metal there is for its weight
Shrugs off seawater and acid
The body does not reject it
cons: Very expensive to separate from its ore

annualProduction.note: almost all of it made from fossil gas and used for ammonia and refining

discovered.era: Henry Cavendish

facts.text: Hydrogen is by far the most abundant element in the universe and a bit player in the crust, where it hides inside water and clay.
Counting atoms rather than mass, hydrogen is roughly 15% of the crust, it is just extremely light.

materials.name: Steel

anthropogenicStock.note: in-use stock worldwide, roughly 4–5 t per person in industrialised countries

tensileStrength.note: mild steel; alloy steels reach 2 GPa

discovered.era: Bessemer converter; crucible and wootz steels far older

facts.text: Steel is the most recycled material on Earth by mass, around 90% of it comes back at end of life.
Making it accounts for roughly 7–9% of global CO2 emissions, almost all of it from using coal to strip oxygen off iron.

pros: Strong when pulled as well as squashed
Recycled endlessly without getting worse
Can be tuned by mixing in other metals
cons: Rusts unless it is coated or alloyed
Making it burns a lot of coal

materials.name: Copper

anthropogenicStock.note: in-use stock, part of the metals category

annualProduction.note: mine production, copper content

discovered.era: The first metal humans worked, found native in usable lumps

facts.text: Copper kills bacteria on contact, which is why hospital door handles are quietly going back to brass.
Electrifying everything runs on copper: a wind turbine holds several tonnes of it, an EV about four times what a petrol car needs.

pros: Carries electricity better than anything affordable
Kills bacteria on contact
Recycled without losing quality
cons: The good ore is running out

materials.name: Zinc

annualProduction.note: mine production, zinc content

discovered.era: Isolated by Marggraf; brass made for millennia before

facts.text: Over half of all zinc goes into galvanising, a sacrificial skin that corrodes so the steel underneath does not.
Zinc is the third metal your body needs most, after iron and, arguably, calcium.

pros: Protects steel by corroding instead of it
Cheap

materials.name: Lead

annualProduction.note: mine production, lead content

discovered.era: Smelted in Anatolia; the Romans plumbed cities with it

facts.text: Around 85% of lead now goes into batteries, and lead-acid batteries are recycled at over 95%, the highest rate of any consumer product.
Ice cores record Roman smelting: atmospheric lead rose across the Empire and fell with it.

pros: Blocks radiation
Recycled at over 95% in batteries

materials.name: Nickel

annualProduction.note: mine production, nickel content

discovered.era: Cronstedt, from an ore miners called 'Old Nick's copper'

facts.text: Nickel is what makes stainless steel stainless, most of it never appears as nickel at all.
The Earth's core is roughly a twentieth nickel, alloyed with iron.

pros: Makes steel stainless
Holds its strength when very hot
cons: Some people react to it on skin

annualProduction.note: mine production, tin content

discovered.era: Bronze Age, tin plus copper started it

facts.text: Tin is scarce and unevenly spread, so Bronze Age trade routes ran thousands of kilometres to fetch it.
Almost half of today's tin is solder, the metal that physically holds electronics together.

materials.name: Gold

anthropogenicStock.note: all gold ever mined, still above ground

discovered.era: Worked from native nuggets before any smelting existed

facts.text: All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube about 22 metres on a side: a single suburban house, filled solid.
One gram can be beaten into a sheet a square metre across, thin enough to see daylight through.
Almost none of it is thrown away; the gold in a Roman coin is probably still in circulation as something else.

pros: Never tarnishes or corrodes
Beaten thinner than any other metal
Almost all of it gets reused
cons: Too soft to be useful pure
Mining it tears up a lot of ground for very little metal

discovered.era: Cupellation from lead ores in Anatolia

facts.text: Silver conducts heat and electricity better than any other element, copper only wins on price.
Solar panels are now one of the largest single consumers of silver, as paste printed onto every cell.

materials.name: Lithium

annualProduction.note: lithium content, excluding US production withheld by USGS

discovered.era: Arfwedson, in a Swedish mineral

facts.text: Lithium is the least dense solid element, it floats on oil, let alone water.
Production has roughly tripled since 2018, driven almost entirely by batteries.

pros: Stores more energy per kilogram than any rival
Lightest solid element there is
cons: Extracting it drains water from dry places

annualProduction.note: usable ore, gross weight

discovered.era: Smelted at the start of the Iron Age, from rock laid down 2.5 billion years earlier

facts.text: Most iron ore was deposited when the first photosynthesising microbes rusted the oceans, an atmospheric catastrophe we now mine.
It is the second-largest bulk cargo on Earth by tonnage moved, after coal.

discovered.era: Named for Les Baux-de-Provence, where it was first described

facts.text: Bauxite is tropical soil that has been rained on for millions of years until only aluminium and iron oxides remain.
It takes roughly four tonnes of bauxite to make one tonne of aluminium, and the leftover red mud is one of the largest industrial waste streams in the world.

annualProduction.note: estimate: limestone quarried for cement, lime and aggregate; not reported as a single global statistic

discovered.era: Quarried for the pyramids

facts.text: Limestone is mostly the compressed bodies of sea creatures, the White Cliffs of Dover are a graveyard of plankton.
Burning it to make cement releases CO2 that was captured by those organisms; that chemistry alone is about half of cement's emissions.

discovered.era: Mined and traded across the Neolithic world

facts.text: Only a small fraction of mined salt is eaten; most goes into chlorine and caustic soda, or onto winter roads.
Salt was money: 'salary' comes from the Roman allowance for buying it.

discovered.era: Plastered onto the walls of Catalhoyuk

facts.text: Gypsum board resists fire because the water chemically bound inside it must boil off before the panel can get hotter than about 100 °C.
Alabaster, plaster of Paris and the walls of most modern houses are all the same mineral in different states of hydration.

annualProduction.note: mostly recovered as a by-product of refining oil and gas

discovered.era: Known to antiquity as brimstone

facts.text: Almost no sulfur is mined any more, it is stripped out of fossil fuels to stop acid rain, then sold.
Sulfuric acid made from it is the single largest-volume industrial chemical on the planet, and most of it makes fertiliser.

discovered.era: First patented as superphosphate fertiliser by Lawes

facts.text: About 70% of the world's phosphate reserves sit in a single country, Morocco, including Western Sahara.
Roughly half the people alive are fed by crops grown with mined phosphate; there is no synthetic substitute.

materials.name: Sand & Gravel

anthropogenicStock.note: aggregates in place, the second-largest human-made stock after concrete

annualProduction.note: 50 Gt/yr of sand, gravel and crushed stone; the most-extracted solid material on Earth

discovered.era: Mixed into the first mud mortars

facts.text: Humans move more sand and gravel than every river on Earth combined.
Desert sand is useless for concrete, wind-rounded grains will not lock together, which is why Dubai imports sand.
It is the second-most consumed resource after water, and almost entirely unregulated.

pros: The cheapest bulk material there is
Needs almost no processing
cons: Dredging it wrecks rivers and coasts
Desert sand is useless for concrete

materials.name: Cement

discovered.era: Joseph Aspdin patents Portland cement; Roman pozzolana far older

facts.text: Cement production is about 8% of global CO2 emissions, more than aviation and shipping together.
China poured more cement in three years than the United States did in the entire twentieth century.

pros: Turns loose rock into solid stone
Cheap and available almost everywhere
cons: About 8% of all carbon dioxide humans emit
Half those emissions come from the chemistry itself, not the fuel

materials.name: Concrete

anthropogenicStock.note: the single largest human-made mass on Earth

annualProduction.note: estimated from cement output at roughly 1:7 by mass. Cement is measured; concrete is not.

tensileStrength.note: about a tenth of its compressive strength, hence rebar

discovered.era: Roman opus caementicium; Portland-cement concrete from 1824

facts.text: There is more concrete on Earth than there are trees, animals and people put together, by mass it outweighs all living things.
Roman harbour concrete gets stronger as seawater reacts with volcanic ash inside it; modern concrete does the opposite.
Nobody measures concrete directly. Every figure you have ever read is cement production multiplied by an assumption.

pros: Enormously strong when squashed
Cheap, and you can pour it into any shape
Does not burn, rot or rust
cons: Cracks easily when pulled or bent
Making the cement in it heats the planet

materials.name: Brick & Fired Clay

annualProduction.note: derived from the growth rate of the brick stock; no single global statistic exists

discovered.era: Sun-dried mud brick in the Levant; fired brick by ~3000 BCE

facts.text: Fired brick is one of the oldest manufactured materials still in daily use, essentially unchanged for five thousand years.
The standard brick size survives because it is what one hand can pick up.

pros: Lasts for thousands of years
Fireproof, and one hand can lift it
cons: Firing the clay takes a lot of fuel

materials.name: Glass

annualProduction.note: container plus flat glass; industry estimate, not an official statistic

meltingPoint.note: working temperature; glass has no true melting point

discovered.era: Mesopotamia; float glass invented 1959

facts.text: Glass is not a slow-flowing liquid. Old cathedral panes are uneven because of how they were spun, not because they sagged.
It can be recycled endlessly with no loss of quality, and a recycled bottle can be back on a shelf within a month.

pros: Lets light through and keeps weather out
Recycled forever with no loss
Nothing sticks to it or leaks through it
cons: A poor insulator on its own

materials.name: Ceramics

annualProduction.note: tiles, sanitaryware, tableware and refractories; industry estimate

thermalConductivity.note: wide range: 2 W/(m·K) for porcelain, 150+ for aluminium nitride

discovered.era: Fired clay figurines from Dolní Věstonice

facts.text: The oldest fired ceramic objects are not pots but figurines, made 26,000 years ago, art preceded tableware by fifteen millennia.
Boron carbide plate stops rifle rounds at a third the weight of the steel that would be needed.

pros: Survives heat that melts metal
Chemically inert and very hard

materials.name: Coal

annualProduction.note: a record year

discovered.era: Burned in Bronze Age China, then Roman Britain

facts.text: Most coal formed in a single 60-million-year window when trees had evolved lignin but fungi had not yet learned to digest it.
Coal use hit an all-time record in 2023, the decline everyone forecast has not started yet.

pros: Dense, cheap energy that needs no refining
Turns iron ore into iron
cons: The single largest source of carbon dioxide
Mining and burning it both kill people

materials.name: Crude Oil

annualProduction.note: about 96 million barrels per day

discovered.era: Drake well, Pennsylvania; seep oil used for millennia

facts.text: Only about 4% of a barrel becomes plastic, but that 4% is where almost every synthetic material in your house comes from.
The world burns roughly 1,500 barrels every second.

pros: Packs enormous energy into a liquid you can pump
The feedstock for nearly every synthetic material
cons: Burning it is the main driver of warming

annualProduction.note: converted from ~4.1 trillion m³ at 0.717 kg/m³

discovered.era: First commercial well, Fredonia, New York

facts.text: Nearly all industrial hydrogen, and therefore nearly all synthetic fertiliser, is made by tearing apart natural gas.
Methane traps about 80 times more heat than CO2 over its first twenty years in the atmosphere.

materials.name: Bitumen

annualProduction.note: refinery bitumen output; industry estimate

discovered.era: Waterproofing Mesopotamian boats and sealing bricks

facts.text: The Pitch Drop Experiment has been running since 1927; bitumen behaves as a solid but flows about one drop per decade.
Asphalt pavement is the most recycled material in the world by weight in several countries, old road is milled straight back into new road.

pros: Waterproof and self-healing under traffic
Milled up and relaid as new road
cons: Softens in heat and cracks in cold

materials.name: Wood

annualProduction.note: converted from 3.97 billion m³ of roundwood at ~0.65 t/m³ air-dry

density.note: 300–850 depending on species; balsa 170, lignum vitae 1250

discovered.era: Wooden tools and spears, long before anything else was made

facts.text: Along the grain, wood beats steel on strength for its weight; across the grain it splits in your hands.
About half of all wood cut worldwide is still burned for cooking and heating.
The Hōryū-ji temple in Japan has been standing in wood since 607 CE.

pros: Grows back, and stores carbon while it does
Strong for its weight
Warm, quiet and easy to cut

materials.name: Paper & Board

discovered.era: Cai Lun, Han dynasty China

facts.text: The paperless office never arrived; packaging board grew as screens replaced letters, because everything now ships in a box.
A cellulose fibre survives roughly five to seven trips through the recycling loop before it is too short to hold together.

pros: Cheap, printable and compostable
Actually recycled, at high rates
cons: Fibres wear out after about five trips
Pulping uses a lot of water and energy

annualProduction.note: wheat, rice, maize and other cereals; grain only, not straw

discovered.era: Domesticated in the Fertile Crescent

facts.text: Three grasses, wheat, rice and maize, supply about half of all calories eaten by humans.
Cereal is the largest deliberately harvested flow of biomass on the planet.

materials.name: Cotton

annualProduction.note: lint

discovered.era: Domesticated independently in India, Peru and Africa

facts.text: A single cotton fibre is stronger than steel of the same weight when wet, cotton gains strength as it soaks.
Around 10,000 litres of water go into one kilogram of cotton; the Aral Sea was drained largely to grow it.

pros: Soft, breathable and absorbent
Biodegrades
Gets stronger when wet
cons: Drinks about 10,000 litres of water per kilogram

materials.name: Wool

annualProduction.note: greasy wool

discovered.era: Sheep bred for fleece in Mesopotamia

facts.text: Wool can hold nearly a third of its weight in water and still feel dry, because the moisture binds inside the fibre.
It is naturally flame-resistant, it chars and self-extinguishes rather than melting.

pros: Warm even when damp
Naturally hard to set alight
Grows back every year
cons: Sheep belch a lot of methane
Shrinks and felts if washed hot

materials.name: Natural Rubber

discovered.era: Goodyear vulcanises it; Mesoamerican rubber ballgames by 1600 BCE

facts.text: No synthetic rubber matches natural latex for heat build-up, so every aircraft and truck tyre still contains tree sap.
Goodyear found vulcanisation by accident, dropping a sulfur-rubber mix on a hot stove.

pros: Stretches and springs back better than any synthetic
Builds up less heat, so tyres last
cons: Only grows in the wet tropics
Perishes in sun, ozone and heat
Some people are allergic to the latex

materials.name: Plastics

discovered.era: Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic

facts.text: Around 9% of all plastic ever made has been recycled. Roughly 12% has been burned. The rest still exists.
Humanity has produced over 9 billion tonnes of plastic since 1950, more than half of it since 2004.
Plastic now outweighs all land and marine animals combined.

pros: Light, cheap and waterproof
Can be moulded into literally any shape
Tough for how little it weighs
cons: Almost none of it is actually recycled
Breaks into fragments that never leave

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total

discovered.era: Found by accident at ICI Northwich under extreme pressure

facts.text: Polyethylene is the most-made synthetic material on Earth: bags, bottles, pipe, and the film over every greenhouse.
It was discovered by accident twice, and kept secret during the war because it insulated radar cabling better than anything else.

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total

discovered.era: Natta, using Ziegler catalysts, a Nobel followed

facts.text: Polypropylene hinges can flex a million times without breaking, which is why the lid of a shampoo bottle is moulded in one piece.
It floats, one of the few common plastics less dense than water, which is how recycling plants sort it.

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total

discovered.era: Observed by Baumann; made workable by Waldo Semon in 1926

facts.text: PVC is over half salt by mass, which makes it the least oil-hungry of the big plastics.
Rigid pipe made from it is expected to last a century underground; the same polymer plasticised becomes a raincoat.

materials.name: PET

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total; excludes polyester fibre

discovered.era: Whinfield and Dickson; the blow-moulded bottle arrives in 1973

facts.text: PET is the only plastic with a genuine bottle-to-bottle recycling loop at scale, and even that mostly ends up as fleece.
Most polyester clothing is the same molecule as a fizzy-drink bottle, spun into thread.

pros: The one plastic with a real bottle-to-bottle loop
Clear, light and shatterproof
cons: Most of it still becomes fleece, not bottles

discovered.era: Bayer's methyl rubber; mass-produced during the Second World War

facts.text: The US built a synthetic rubber industry from nothing in three years after Japan took the rubber plantations of South-East Asia.
A car tyre is a composite of a dozen rubbers, steel cord and textile, which is exactly why tyres are so hard to recycle.

materials.name: Graphite

annualProduction.note: natural graphite; synthetic graphite adds roughly as much again

thermalConductivity.note: in-plane; about 30 times lower through the sheets

discovered.era: Borrowdale deposit, England, the first pencils

facts.text: Graphite is slippery because its carbon sheets slide over each other; a pencil line is those sheets peeling off one at a time.
The anode of every lithium-ion battery is graphite, so there is more of it in an EV than there is lithium.
Graphite and diamond are the same element; the difference is entirely how the atoms are stacked.

pros: Slippery and heat-proof at once
The anode in every lithium battery
cons: Mining and shaping it is dusty work
Supply is concentrated in very few countries

materials.name: Carbon Fibre

annualProduction.note: industry estimate; no official statistic

discovered.era: High-strength process developed at RAE Farnborough

facts.text: A single filament is about 6 micrometres across, roughly a tenth the width of a human hair.
Half the structural mass of a Boeing 787 is carbon composite, which is also why a damaged panel cannot simply be beaten out.
It is essentially unrecyclable: the fibres survive, the epoxy does not, and separating them costs more than new fibre.

pros: Stiffer and stronger than steel at a third the weight
Does not fatigue or rust
cons: Shatters rather than dents on impact

materials.name: Graphene

annualProduction.note: market estimate, wide error bars; most output is multi-layer flake, not true monolayer

discovered.era: Geim and Novoselov, peeled off graphite with sticky tape

facts.text: A sheet of graphene as thin as cling film could support an elephant standing on a pencil point, if you could make one that big without a single flaw.
It was isolated with ordinary adhesive tape, and that experiment won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Twenty years on, the flaw-free sheet remains the whole problem: production is measured in tonnes, not megatonnes.

pros: The strongest material ever measured
Conducts heat better than anything known
Transparent and flexible at once
cons: Nobody can make large flawless sheets
Still measured in tonnes, not megatonnes

discovered.era: Isolated by Gahn

facts.text: Steel without manganese is unworkably brittle; every tonne of it carries a few kilograms of the stuff.

annualProduction.note: chromite ore, gross weight

discovered.era: Isolated by Vauquelin

facts.text: Chromium is what makes stainless steel stainless: it grows an invisible oxide skin that heals itself.

discovered.era: Isolated by Brandt

facts.text: Most cobalt is a by-product of copper and nickel mining, and about 70% of it comes from one country.

discovered.era: Isolated by Hjelm

facts.text: Adding a little molybdenum lets steel keep its strength red-hot, which is why jet engines and pipelines use it.

discovered.era: Isolated by the Elhuyar brothers

facts.text: Tungsten melts at 3,422 °C, higher than any other metal, it was the filament in every light bulb for a century.

discovered.era: Rediscovered by Sefström

facts.text: A few kilograms of vanadium per tonne doubles the strength of steel; the Ford Model T was built of it.

discovered.era: Ground into kohl and painted around Egyptian eyes

facts.text: Antimony has been painted around eyes since ancient Egypt; today most of it is a flame retardant.

discovered.era: Finally told apart from lead

facts.text: Bismuth grows staircase crystals in rainbow colours, and it is the heaviest element that is not meaningfully radioactive.

discovered.era: Isolated by Stromeyer

facts.text: Cadmium is entirely a by-product of zinc smelting, nobody mines it on purpose.

discovered.era: Found sealed in Egyptian tombs

facts.text: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature, and the only one banned by a treaty named after a city.

discovered.era: The first of the seventeen; the last was not separated until 1945

facts.text: They are not actually rare, they are just never concentrated, so separating the seventeen of them takes hundreds of chemical steps.

materials.name: Uranium

discovered.era: Isolated by Klaproth

facts.text: A single kilogram of uranium holds as much energy as about 3,000 tonnes of coal.

pros: A kilogram holds the energy of 3,000 tonnes of coal
Generates power without carbon dioxide
cons: The waste stays dangerous for a very long time
The same material can be made into weapons

discovered.era: Named, though pre-Columbian Ecuador was working it long before

facts.text: Spanish colonists threw platinum away as 'little silver' that would not melt, their furnaces could not reach 1,768 °C.

discovered.era: Isolated by Wollaston

facts.text: Palladium can soak up 900 times its own volume in hydrogen gas, like a metal sponge.

discovered.era: Isolated by Ekeberg

facts.text: Almost every phone holds a speck of tantalum: it makes the smallest capacitors that store the most charge.

discovered.era: Isolated by Hatchett

facts.text: One country, Brazil, supplies about 90% of the world's niobium.

discovered.era: Identified by Klaproth; single grains of it are 4.4 billion years old

facts.text: The oldest known piece of Earth is a zircon crystal from Australia, older than the oceans.

discovered.era: Isolated by Boisbaudran

facts.text: Gallium melts in your hand at 30 °C, a spoon made of it disappears into a hot drink.

discovered.era: Discovered by its indigo spectral line

facts.text: Every touchscreen is coated in indium tin oxide, a metal film that conducts electricity and lets light through.

discovered.era: Isolated by Berzelius

facts.text: Selenium's electrical resistance drops in light, which is how the first photocopiers and light meters worked.

discovered.era: Burned for mortar and plaster

facts.text: Lime is limestone cooked until the carbon dioxide leaves; add water and it sets back into stone.

discovered.era: Leblanc process; the Solvay process replaced it in 1861

facts.text: Soda ash is what lowers the melting point of sand enough to make glass in an ordinary furnace.

annualProduction.note: K2O equivalent

discovered.era: Leached from wood ash in iron pots, which is where the name comes from

facts.text: Potash is the K in NPK fertiliser, and it is mostly the dried remains of ancient inland seas.

discovered.era: Used as a smelting flux

facts.text: Most barite goes down oil wells: it is heavy enough to hold back the pressure of the rock.

discovered.era: Element isolated, borax had travelled the Silk Road for centuries

facts.text: Borosilicate glass survives a hot oven because boron shrinks how much it expands when heated.

discovered.era: Described by Agricola as a flux that makes ore run

facts.text: Fluorspar glows under ultraviolet light, and the word fluorescence is named after it.

discovered.era: Fired into the first true porcelain in China

facts.text: The same white clay that makes porcelain also makes glossy magazine paper glossy.

discovered.era: Named after Fort Benton, Wyoming

facts.text: Bentonite swells to many times its dry volume in water, which is why it seals landfills and cat litter alike.

discovered.era: Carved as soapstone

facts.text: Talc is the softest mineral there is, it defines 1 on the hardness scale, and your fingernail beats it.

discovered.era: Named; it had been in pottery glazes for millennia

facts.text: About half of the Earth's crust is feldspar, which makes it the most common material on the planet that almost nobody can name.

annualProduction.note: industrial-grade silica sand only, separate from construction aggregate; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Melted into the first glass in Mesopotamia

facts.text: Glass, silicon chips and fracking all need sand far purer than the stuff on a beach.

discovered.era: Split into windows for lanterns and furnaces

facts.text: Mica splits into sheets a fraction of a millimetre thick that are transparent and will not burn.

discovered.era: Named

facts.text: Burnt magnesite lines the inside of steel furnaces, because it does not melt until about 2,800 °C.

discovered.era: Commercialised

facts.text: Heat perlite and the water trapped inside pops it like popcorn, to twenty times its volume.

discovered.era: Nobel used it to make nitroglycerine safe

facts.text: Diatomite is the glass skeletons of microscopic algae, piled up over millions of years. Dynamite is nitroglycerine soaked into it.

discovered.era: Named for the worm shapes it makes when heated

facts.text: Heated fast, vermiculite unrolls into worm-shaped strands, the name comes from the Latin for little worm.

discovered.era: Discovered in seaweed ash

facts.text: Adding iodine to table salt is one of the cheapest public-health measures ever invented.

discovered.era: Isolated by Balard

facts.text: Bromine is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature, and it is drawn straight out of brine.

materials.name: Helium

annualProduction.note: converted from about 160 million cubic metres a year at 0.1786 kg/m3; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Found in the Sun's spectrum, before anyone found it on Earth

facts.text: Helium was discovered on the Sun before it was found on Earth, and once it escapes the atmosphere it is gone for good.

pros: The coldest useful coolant there is
Chemically inert and non-flammable
cons: Once it escapes, it leaves the planet for good

materials.name: Asbestos

discovered.era: Woven into fireproof cloth by the ancients

facts.text: Asbestos is a rock that can be spun into fireproof thread, and the same needle-fine fibres that make it useful make it deadly.

pros: Fireproof, and it can be spun into cloth
Cheap and extremely durable
cons: The fibres cause fatal lung disease
Banned in most of the world

materials.name: Ammonia

discovered.era: Haber–Bosch process

facts.text: About half the nitrogen atoms in your body were pulled out of the air by the Haber–Bosch process. Roughly half the world eats because of it.

pros: Feeds roughly half the people alive
Carries hydrogen in liquid form

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: First organic compound made from inorganic parts

facts.text: Urea was the first 'living' molecule made in a lab from dead chemicals, which quietly ended the idea of a life force.

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Distilled by alchemists as oil of vitriol

facts.text: A country's sulfuric acid output was once used as a measure of how industrialised it was. Most of it goes into fertiliser.

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Made by electrolysing brine

facts.text: Caustic soda and chlorine come out of the same machine: split salt water and you get one of each, whether you wanted both or not.

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Isolated by Scheele

facts.text: Chlorinating drinking water is reckoned to have added decades to average life expectancy.

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Made by distilling wood until the 1920s

facts.text: Methanol used to be made by roasting wood, which is why it is still called wood alcohol.

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Cracked out of petroleum

facts.text: Ethylene is the most-made organic chemical on Earth, and it is also the gas ripening fruit gives off.

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: By-product of petroleum cracking

facts.text: Propylene is mostly a leftover of making ethylene, and it becomes the plastic in bottle caps and car bumpers.

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Isolated by Faraday

facts.text: Kekulé said he worked out benzene's ring shape after dreaming of a snake biting its own tail.

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total

discovered.era: Made commercially

facts.text: Expanded polystyrene is 98% air, which is why a big block of it weighs almost nothing.

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Invented by Bayer

facts.text: The same chemistry makes mattress foam, skateboard wheels and the varnish on a wooden floor.

materials.name: Nylon

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Announced by DuPont

facts.text: Nylon stockings sold four million pairs in four days in 1940, then vanished into parachutes for the war.

pros: Tough, elastic and abrasion resistant
Holds a shape when spun into thread

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Developed in the 1940s

facts.text: Every Lego brick is ABS, moulded to within two-thousandths of a millimetre so bricks from 1958 still fit today.

annualProduction.note: subset of the plastics total; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Commercialised

facts.text: Epoxy is the glue that holds carbon fibre together, without it a wing would just be a bundle of threads.

discovered.era: Domesticated in New Guinea

facts.text: Sugarcane is the single largest crop on Earth by weight, and most of it is water and fibre rather than sugar.

annualProduction.note: part of the cereals total

discovered.era: Bred from a wild grass in Mexico

facts.text: Most maize is never eaten by people: it feeds animals, fills fuel tanks and turns into syrup.

annualProduction.note: part of the cereals total

discovered.era: Domesticated in the Fertile Crescent

facts.text: Bread rises because wheat, almost alone among grains, has enough gluten to trap the gas that yeast makes.

annualProduction.note: paddy rice; part of the cereals total

discovered.era: Domesticated in the Yangtze valley

facts.text: Rice feeds more people than any other single food, and growing it in flooded paddies produces a tenth of farming's methane.

discovered.era: Domesticated in the Andes

facts.text: Potatoes gave Europe so many more calories per field that historians credit them with a quarter of its population growth.

discovered.era: Domesticated in China

facts.text: Soy is the cheapest protein there is, and most of it is fed to animals rather than people.

materials.name: Palm Oil

discovered.era: Pressed in West Africa; plantations arrived in the 1900s

facts.text: Palm oil yields more oil per hectare than any other crop, which is both why it is everywhere and why forests fall for it.

pros: Yields more oil per hectare than any other crop
Solid at room temperature without hydrogen
cons: Habitat loss for orangutans and elephants

discovered.era: Herded animals milked from about this point

facts.text: Most adults on Earth cannot digest milk; the ability to do so is a recent mutation that spread with herding.

discovered.era: Hunted forever; farmed from about this point

facts.text: There are roughly three chickens alive for every person, and by weight farmed birds outweigh all wild birds several times over.

discovered.era: Fished since the Stone Age; farmed fish overtook the wild catch in the 2010s

facts.text: More fish now comes from farms than from the sea, the crossover happened in the 2010s.

discovered.era: Hens domesticated in South-East Asia

facts.text: An eggshell is calcium carbonate, the same mineral as limestone, built by the hen in about twenty hours.

discovered.era: Cultivated in Ethiopia and Yemen

facts.text: Coffee is one of the most traded farm goods in the world, and every plant descends from a small patch of Ethiopian forest.

discovered.era: Spun in Bengal; industrialised in the 1800s

facts.text: Jute is the cheapest natural fibre after cotton, and a sack of it rots away instead of becoming litter.

materials.name: Silk

discovered.era: Reeled in China, and kept a state secret for millennia

facts.text: One cocoon unwinds into a single thread up to 900 metres long, and the method was a Chinese state secret for millennia.

pros: Stronger than steel thread of the same weight
Smooth, light and warm

annualProduction.note: made from roundwood

discovered.era: Ground-wood pulping from the 1840s

facts.text: Paper was made from rags until someone worked out how to grind wood into fibre, which is when books got cheap.

annualProduction.note: converted from about 500 million cubic metres at roughly 0.6 t/m3; part of the roundwood total

discovered.era: Sawn planks in Egypt; water-powered sawmills from the 1200s

facts.text: A plank is stronger for its weight than steel along the grain, and useless across it.

materials.name: Leather

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Tanning is one of the oldest chemical processes we know

facts.text: Tanning turns skin into a material that will not rot, and it is one of the oldest chemical processes we know.

pros: Tough, breathable, and lasts decades
Moulds to whatever it is shaped around
cons: Comes with the footprint of raising cattle

materials.name: Water

annualProduction.note: Fresh water withdrawn worldwide each year. The 106 Gt headline counts solid materials only, so this sits outside it; adding the two together would be comparing different censuses.

discovered.era: Longer ago than anything else here; our ancestors drank and carried it before they made a single thing

facts.text: By weight humans move more water than every other material put together, roughly forty times over.

pros: Dissolves more substances than any other liquid
Carries heat away better than almost anything
Free where it rains
cons: Heavy and expensive to move any distance
Most of the world's supply is salt or frozen
Farming takes seven litres of it for every ten used

materials.name: Stainless Steel

annualProduction.note: part of the crude steel total; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Harry Brearley notices a gun-barrel steel that will not rust

facts.text: Stainless steel does not resist rust so much as rust instantly: a chromium oxide skin forms in seconds and seals the surface.

pros: Does not rust, stain or need painting
Safe for food and surgery
Recycled like any other steel
cons: Several times the price of plain steel
Needs chromium and nickel, both mined far away

materials.name: Cast Iron

annualProduction.note: iron castings only; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Poured in China, some 1,500 years before Europe managed it

facts.text: Cast iron holds so much carbon that it cannot be hammered into shape at all. It has to be poured.

pros: Pours into complicated shapes cheaply
Soaks up vibration
Wears extremely well
cons: Cannot be forged or easily welded

materials.name: Bronze

annualProduction.note: copper-tin alloy semis; consensus estimate

discovered.era: The alloy that named an age

facts.text: Bronze gave its name to an entire age because it was the first metal humans deliberately mixed rather than simply found.

pros: Harder than either metal it is made from
Does not spark, and shrugs off seawater
Casts beautifully
cons: Tin is scarce and was traded across continents to get it

materials.name: Brass

annualProduction.note: copper-zinc alloy semis; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Made before anyone knew zinc was an element

facts.text: Brass was made for centuries before zinc was identified, by smelting copper with a zinc ore and hoping.

pros: Machines more easily than almost any metal
Kills bacteria on contact
Looks like gold for none of the price

materials.name: Solder

annualProduction.note: electronics solder; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Used to join gold in Mesopotamia

facts.text: Solder is the material that physically holds electronics together, and switching it away from lead in the 2000s forced every factory on Earth to retool.

pros: Melts far below the metals it joins
Conducts electricity across the joint
Repairable with a cheap iron
cons: Joints crack under vibration and thermal cycling

materials.name: Beryllium

discovered.era: Isolated by Vauquelin from emerald

facts.text: Beryllium is stiffer than steel at a quarter the weight, and it is transparent to X-rays, which is why detector windows are made of it.

pros: Stiffest metal there is for its weight
Lets X-rays straight through
Does not spark
cons: The dust causes an incurable lung disease

materials.name: Germanium

discovered.era: Found by Winkler, exactly where Mendeleev predicted a gap

facts.text: The first transistor was germanium, not silicon. Silicon won because its oxide made a better insulator.

pros: Sees infrared light that silicon cannot
Faster than silicon for some circuits
cons: Scarce, and only a by-product of zinc and coal

materials.name: Tellurium

discovered.era: Found in Transylvanian gold ore

facts.text: Tellurium is rarer in the crust than platinum, and most of what we get comes from the sludge left at the bottom of copper refineries.

pros: Makes a thin-film solar cell that beats silicon on cost
Turns heat straight into electricity
cons: Supply depends entirely on how much copper is refined

materials.name: Rhenium

discovered.era: The last stable element to be discovered

facts.text: Rhenium was the last stable element found on Earth, and jet engine blades are the reason anyone bothers to extract it.

pros: Keeps its strength almost to its melting point
Lets jet engines run hotter, so they burn less fuel
cons: One of the rarest elements in the crust

materials.name: Strontium

discovered.era: Named after Strontian, a village in Scotland

facts.text: Strontium is what makes fireworks red, and it is named after a Scottish village of about 300 people.

pros: The only cheap source of a true red flame
Blocks X-rays in glass
cons: Its radioactive isotope is a notorious fallout product
Few uses left since cathode-ray televisions died

materials.name: Arsenic

discovered.era: Isolated by Albertus Magnus

facts.text: Arsenic is a by-product nobody wants: it comes out of copper and gold smelting whether or not there is a buyer.

pros: Hardens lead for shot and batteries
Makes semiconductors that are faster than silicon
cons: Contaminates groundwater for millions of people

materials.name: Neodymium

annualProduction.note: part of the rare earth total; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Split from didymium by von Welsbach

facts.text: A neodymium magnet the size of a coin can lift a small child, and every wind turbine and earbud depends on them.

pros: By far the strongest permanent magnet known
Makes motors smaller and lighter
cons: Supply is concentrated in one country

materials.name: Rhodium

discovered.era: Isolated by Wollaston from crude platinum

facts.text: Rhodium is the most expensive metal on Earth by weight, and almost all of it sits in car exhausts turning nitrogen oxides back into air.

pros: The best catalyst known for cleaning exhaust gases
Never tarnishes
cons: Mined in only a couple of places on Earth

materials.name: Zirconium

discovered.era: Isolated by Berzelius

facts.text: Zirconium lets neutrons pass straight through it, which is why the fuel rods in almost every nuclear reactor are sheathed in it.

pros: Nearly invisible to neutrons
Shrugs off hot water and acid
Accepted by the body as an implant
cons: Reacts violently with steam if a reactor overheats

materials.name: Fly Ash

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: First blended into concrete in the United States

facts.text: Fly ash is what is left in the chimney after burning coal, and stirring it into concrete both cuts cement use and hides the waste.

pros: Replaces cement, which cuts a lot of carbon dioxide
Makes concrete denser and more durable
It is waste, so it is cheap
cons: Supply disappears as coal plants close
Quality varies from plant to plant

materials.name: Slag

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: As old as smelting itself, and thrown away for most of that time

facts.text: Every tonne of iron leaves about a third of a tonne of slag. It was spoil for three thousand years; now it is ground up and sold as cement.

pros: Replaces cement almost one for one
Makes concrete resist seawater
Turns a waste heap into a product
cons: Only exists where blast furnaces do

materials.name: Dimension Stone

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Quarried in blocks for the pyramids and everything since

facts.text: Dimension stone is rock cut into shapes rather than crushed, and the saw does more damage than the quarry: over half the block ends up as dust.

pros: Lasts for thousands of years with no maintenance
Needs no processing beyond cutting
Every piece is different
cons: More than half the block is wasted in cutting

materials.name: Plywood

annualProduction.note: converted from roughly 120 million cubic metres at about 0.65 t/m3

discovered.era: Rotary-peeled veneer makes it cheap

facts.text: Gluing thin sheets with their grain crossed cancels out wood's biggest weakness: plywood is nearly as strong across as along.

pros: Strong in both directions, unlike plain wood
Comes in big flat sheets
Does not split when nailed near an edge

materials.name: Particleboard & MDF

annualProduction.note: converted from roughly 150 million cubic metres of wood-based panels

discovered.era: Developed to use sawmill waste during wartime shortages

facts.text: Particleboard was invented to use up sawdust, and most flat-pack furniture is still sawdust glued back into the shape of a plank.

pros: Made from offcuts and sawdust
Perfectly flat and cheap
Takes a printed finish well
cons: Swells and crumbles once water gets in
Will not hold a screw twice

materials.name: Bamboo

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Built with across Asia for as long as there have been houses there

facts.text: Bamboo is a grass, not a tree, and some species grow nearly a metre a day. It is ready to cut in four years rather than forty.

pros: Grows back in years rather than decades
Stronger in tension than most timber
Needs no replanting after cutting
cons: Rots and gets eaten unless treated

materials.name: Mineral Wool

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Spun from molten slag in Wales

facts.text: Mineral wool is rock spun into candy floss. It is 98% trapped air, which is what actually does the insulating.

pros: Does not burn
Deadens sound as well as heat
Made partly from slag

materials.name: Glass Fibre

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Drawn accidentally at Owens-Illinois

facts.text: Glass is brittle in a block and springy in a thread: drawn thin enough, the flaws that make it shatter simply are not there.

pros: Stronger than steel wire for its weight
A fraction of the price of carbon fibre
Does not rot or rust
cons: Bends much more easily than carbon fibre
The dust irritates skin and lungs
Hard to recycle once set in resin

materials.name: Titanium Dioxide

discovered.era: Replaces white lead in paint

facts.text: Titanium dioxide is the whitest thing there is. It is in paint, sunscreen, toothpaste and the icing on doughnuts.

pros: Whiter and more opaque than any alternative
Blocks ultraviolet light
Replaced poisonous white lead
cons: Making it produces a lot of acidic waste
Being reassessed for safety as a food colour

materials.name: Carbon Black

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Ground from lamp soot for ink

facts.text: Nearly a third of a car tyre by weight is carbon black. Without it rubber would wear out in a few hundred miles.

pros: Makes rubber last many times longer
The blackest cheap pigment there is
Blocks ultraviolet damage
cons: Made by burning oil in short supply of air
The dust is a workplace hazard
Makes rubber almost impossible to recycle cleanly

materials.name: Ethanol

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Fermented in China long before anyone distilled it

facts.text: Most ethanol made today is not drunk. It is burned in car engines, mostly from maize and sugarcane.

pros: Made from crops rather than oil
Burns cleanly and boosts octane
Mixes straight into petrol
cons: Uses cropland that could grow food
Absorbs water, which corrodes fuel systems
Holds a third less energy than petrol

materials.name: Nitric Acid

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Distilled by alchemists as aqua fortis

facts.text: Nitric acid made from ammonia is how nitrogen from the air becomes fertiliser, and also how it becomes explosives. The same plant can do either.

pros: Turns ammonia into fertiliser the soil can use
Dissolves most metals, which is how they are refined
cons: Its production releases nitrous oxide, a very strong greenhouse gas

materials.name: Phosphoric Acid

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: First made by Scheele from bone ash

facts.text: The tang in a cola is phosphoric acid, the same chemical that turns phosphate rock into fertiliser.

pros: The route from rock to usable fertiliser
Stops rust when brushed onto steel
Safe enough to drink in tiny amounts
cons: Leaves mountains of mildly radioactive phosphogypsum

materials.name: Styrene

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Distilled from storax resin by Simon

facts.text: Styrene was first pulled out of tree resin, and it still smells sweet enough that people used to describe it as pleasant.

pros: Polymerises into a clear, rigid, cheap plastic
Easy to make from two commodity chemicals
cons: Polymerises on its own if it is not kept cool

materials.name: Butadiene

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: First prepared by Caventou

facts.text: Butadiene is the molecule that makes synthetic rubber possible, and building a supply of it was a wartime priority for both sides.

pros: The backbone of synthetic rubber
A by-product of making ethylene, so it is cheap
cons: Explosive, and it forms unstable peroxides in storage

materials.name: Paraxylene

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Separated from coal tar

facts.text: Almost every polyester shirt and drinks bottle starts as paraxylene, a clear liquid that smells faintly of petrol.

pros: The single feedstock behind all polyester
Separated cleanly by freezing its isomers out
cons: Separating it from its near-identical twins takes a lot of energy

materials.name: Formaldehyde

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Discovered by Butlerov

facts.text: Formaldehyde is the glue in most plywood and chipboard, which is why a new flat-pack wardrobe has a smell.

pros: The cheapest strong wood glue there is
Preserves biological tissue indefinitely
cons: Slowly leaks out of the boards it is glued into

materials.name: Acetic Acid

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Made by letting wine go sour

facts.text: Vinegar and industrial acetic acid are the same molecule; one is 5% in water and the other is nearly pure.

pros: Safe enough to eat when diluted
The starting point for most polyester and paint

materials.name: Soap & Detergents

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Boiled from fat and ash in Babylon

facts.text: Soap works because one end of the molecule likes water and the other likes grease, so it drags dirt into the rinse.

pros: Hand washing with it is among the cheapest lifesavers ever found
Works in cold water
cons: Some kinds feed algal blooms in rivers

materials.name: Paint & Coatings

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Ochre handprints on cave walls

facts.text: Paint is mostly a way of stopping other materials from rotting. The colour is close to a side effect.

pros: Adds decades to the life of steel and timber
Cheap protection per square metre

materials.name: Polyester Fibre

annualProduction.note: counted apart from the plastics total, which excludes textile fibres; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Spun by Whinfield and Dickson

facts.text: More than half of all clothing made today is polyester, which means most wardrobes are mostly oil.

pros: Cheap, strong and does not crease
Dries fast and holds colour
Can be made from recycled bottles
cons: Sheds plastic microfibres in every wash

materials.name: Viscose

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Patented by Cross, Bevan and Beadle

facts.text: Viscose is wood dissolved into syrup and squirted back out as thread. It is not synthetic and not natural.

pros: Feels like silk at a fraction of the price
Made from a crop that grows back
Biodegrades
cons: The classic process uses carbon disulfide, which poisoned generations of workers
Some of the pulp comes from old-growth forest

materials.name: Polycarbonate

annualProduction.note: part of the plastics total; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Found independently at Bayer and General Electric within a week

facts.text: Polycarbonate is glass-clear and nearly unbreakable, which is why riot shields and headlamps are made of it.

pros: Almost impossible to shatter
Clear as glass but far lighter
Survives being bent

materials.name: PTFE

annualProduction.note: part of the plastics total; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Found by accident by Roy Plunkett

facts.text: Nothing sticks to PTFE, including glue, which made getting it to stay on a frying pan a harder problem than inventing it.

pros: The slipperiest solid known
Shrugs off almost every chemical
Works from deep cold to 260 degrees
cons: Gives off toxic fumes if overheated

materials.name: Silicone

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Commercialised by Dow Corning

facts.text: Silicone has a backbone of silicon and oxygen rather than carbon, which is why it survives heat that destroys ordinary rubber.

pros: Stays flexible from freezing to baking
Does not react with the body
Repels water completely
cons: Costs many times more than rubber

materials.name: Acrylic

annualProduction.note: part of the plastics total; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Marketed as Plexiglas

facts.text: Acrylic passes more light than glass and does not shatter, which is why aquarium walls holding whole whale sharks are made of it.

pros: Clearer than glass, and half the weight
Does not yellow outdoors
Cuts and bends easily
cons: Scratches far more easily than glass

materials.name: PLA

annualProduction.note: part of the plastics total; consensus estimate

discovered.era: Commercialised from fermented starch

facts.text: PLA is plastic made from maize sugar, and it is what most desktop 3D printers extrude.

pros: Made from crops, not oil
Composts in an industrial digester
Prints and moulds at low heat
cons: Will not break down in a garden heap or the sea

materials.name: Aramid Fibre

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Invented by Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont

facts.text: Kevlar was discovered when a cloudy solution that any chemist would have thrown out was spun anyway, and came out five times stronger than steel.

pros: Five times the tensile strength of steel by weight
Does not melt or burn
Absorbs impact instead of shattering

materials.name: Cassava

discovered.era: Domesticated in Brazil

facts.text: Cassava feeds around 800 million people and is poisonous until it is properly processed.

pros: Grows on poor soil where little else will
Keeps in the ground until it is needed
Enormous calorie yield per hectare
cons: Contains cyanide compounds until prepared correctly

annualProduction.note: part of the cereals total

discovered.era: Domesticated in the Fertile Crescent alongside wheat

facts.text: Barley was the grain of the ancient world: workers on the pyramids were paid in bread and beer made from it.

annualProduction.note: part of the cereals total

discovered.era: Domesticated in Sudan

facts.text: Sorghum keeps growing when maize gives up: it can wait out a drought and start again when the rain comes.

discovered.era: Domesticated in Mesoamerica; reached Europe in the 1500s

facts.text: Europeans grew tomatoes as ornaments for two centuries before they trusted them enough to eat.

discovered.era: Domesticated in New Guinea

facts.text: Almost every banana exported is a clone of one variety, which is why a single fungus can threaten the entire trade.

discovered.era: Grown in India and China for lamp oil

facts.text: Rapeseed was a lamp oil and an engine lubricant long before plant breeders made a version that was pleasant to eat.

discovered.era: Domesticated in North America

facts.text: A sunflower head is not one flower but up to two thousand, packed in the tightest spiral that geometry allows.

discovered.era: Carried across the Pacific by boat and by tide

facts.text: A coconut can float across an ocean and still sprout when it lands, which is how it colonised most tropical coasts.

discovered.era: Drunk in Mesoamerica, long before anyone made it sweet

facts.text: Cocoa beans were money in the Aztec world: a hundred of them bought a turkey.

discovered.era: Drunk in China

facts.text: Black, green and white tea all come from the same plant. The difference is entirely how long the leaf is allowed to oxidise.

materials.name: Refined Sugar

discovered.era: Crystallised in India

facts.text: Sugar was a medicine sold by the spoonful in medieval Europe, and it stayed a luxury until slavery made it cheap.

pros: Preserves food indefinitely
Pure, cheap energy
Keeps for years without spoiling
cons: Its history is bound up with slavery

annualProduction.note: made from part of the milk total

discovered.era: Strained in pottery sieves in Poland

facts.text: Cheese is a way of storing milk. Ten litres of it become one kilogram that keeps for months.

materials.name: Tobacco

discovered.era: Cultivated in the Americas

facts.text: Tobacco funded the founding of several colonies, and it is the only widely sold crop that kills a large share of the people who use it as intended.

pros: Grows on land too poor for food crops
Was a currency in colonial America
cons: Kills over seven million people a year
Curing it burns a lot of firewood

materials.name: Hemp

discovered.era: Spun into cord in China

facts.text: Sails, ropes and the first paper were hemp. The word canvas comes from cannabis.

pros: Grows fast with little water and no pesticide
Very strong fibre
Improves the soil it grows in
cons: Banned for decades because of its relatives

discovered.era: Woven in Georgia, the oldest known cloth

facts.text: The oldest known fabric is linen, spun from wild flax about 34,000 years ago.

discovered.era: Used by the Maya for rope

facts.text: Sisal comes from an agave, a cousin of the plant that makes tequila.

discovered.era: Twisted into rope by Indian Ocean sailors

facts.text: Coir is the hairy husk of a coconut, and it is one of the few natural fibres that does not rot in seawater.

materials.name: Cork

annualProduction.note: consensus estimate; no free official statistic

discovered.era: Stoppering amphorae in the Mediterranean

facts.text: Cork is bark, and the tree survives being stripped. A cork oak can be harvested every nine years for two centuries.

pros: Harvested without felling the tree
Floats, insulates and seals at once
Fully biodegradable
cons: Only grows around the western Mediterranean
